Pure Religion
PYUR ree-LIJ-un
noun phrase
Greek threskeia katharos (θρησκεία καθαρόσ) — from threskeia (religion, worship, the outward practice of piety) and katharos (pure, clean, unmixed, without impurity). The English word religion derives from Latin religio (conscientiousness, awe, the binding obligation of piety; from relegere or religare, to bind again). Together, “pure religion” names the worship that is uncontaminated by self-deception and unmixed with worldliness — worship that produces visible covenant faithfulness.

Biblical Definition

Pure religion is the phrase James uses to define genuine, God-honoring piety in contrast to the self-deceptive religion that hears the word but does not do it (Jas 1:22–27). The definition is concrete and double: “Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their distress — and to keep oneself unstained by the world” (Jas 1:27).

The two clauses are inseparable. The first — visiting orphans and widows in their distress — names the active, outward expression of covenant love toward those who have no natural protector. This is not a peripheral addendum to religion but its index; the prophets measured Israel's covenant faithfulness precisely by how it treated the powerless (Isa 1:17; Jer 22:16; Micah 6:8). The second clause — keeping oneself unstained by the world — names the inward, passive form of purity: the refusal of the entanglements that corrupt the soul and compromise the testimony. Both together constitute genuine piety: active mercy toward the vulnerable, and active self-preservation from worldly corruption.

The contrast James draws is with the person who thinks himself religious but does not bridle his tongue (Jas 1:26) — whose religion is inward pretense rather than outward covenant faithfulness. The Psalms ground the prerequisite: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who has not lifted up his soul to an idol, nor sworn deceitfully” (Ps 24:4). Christ confronted the same hollow religion in the Pharisees: “you have neglected the weightier provisions of the Law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (Matt 23:23). Pure religion is the integration of these three: right worship before God, just dealings with people, and mercy toward the vulnerable.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defined religion as “the recognition of God as an object of worship, love and obedience; right practice in relation to God; piety” and distinguished “pure religion” as that which is uncontaminated by hypocrisy, superstition, or worldliness — religion that matches its inner profession with outward covenant faithfulness.

RELIGION, n. [L. religio, from religo, to bind anew; re and ligo.] The recognition of God as an object of worship, love and obedience; right practice in relation to God and man; a life of piety.

Religion consists in two things: the belief of the divine character and will, and the obedience of that will. Without this, religion is mere formality. With it, it produces the pure religion James describes.

Pure religion, as James defines it (Jas 1:27), is distinguished from vain religion by its outward fruits: visiting the fatherless and the widow in their affliction, and keeping oneself unspotted from the world.

Key Scripture

Jas 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their distress — and to keep oneself unstained by the world."

Ps 24:4 — "He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who has not lifted up his soul to an idol, nor sworn deceitfully."

Matt 23:23 — "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites — because you pay tithe of mint and dill and cummin, and have neglected the weightier provisions of the Law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. But these are the things you should have done — without neglecting the others."

Micah 6:8 — "He has shown you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?"

Modern Corruption

Progressive Christianity reduces pure religion to social activism — especially on politically favored causes — while stripping the second clause of James 1:27 (keeping oneself unstained by the world) as if personal holiness were irrelevant to genuine piety.

expand to see more

Liberation theology and progressive evangelicalism have weaponized James 1:27 into a mandate for political activism on behalf of approved victim categories, treating “visiting orphans and widows” as the whole of genuine religion while quietly setting aside “keeping oneself unstained by the world.” The result is a religion that is active on behalf of the politically fashionable poor while accommodating every form of worldliness in lifestyle, sexuality, and doctrine. This is precisely the selective piety Christ condemned in Matthew 23:23: tithing spices while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness. Half of James 1:27 is not pure religion; it is a redefined religion that substitutes social solidarity for personal holiness.

Fundamentalism offered a mirror corruption: obsessive attention to personal separation from worldly behaviors while neglecting the prophetic tradition's demand for justice toward the vulnerable. A piety that avoids movies and dances while ignoring the widow next door and the orphan in the foster system has equally violated the definition James gives. The Reformers, the Puritans, and the great nineteenth-century Reformed evangelicals (Wilberforce, Whitefield) refused this bifurcation: mercy toward the poor and personal holiness were integrated, not competitive; the same gospel that cleanses the heart drives the hand toward those in distress.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek threskeia (religious practice) and katharos (pure, unmixed) together define religion that is genuine — unmixed with self-deception — and visible in covenant mercy toward the vulnerable.

expand to see more

Greek threskeia (θρησκεία) — religious practice, worship, piety; specifically the outward expression of religion as a system of observances; James uses it neutrally in 1:26–27, distinguishing the vain form (bridleless tongue) from the pure form (mercy and holiness)

Greek katharos (καθαρόσ) — pure, clean, unmixed; used of grain without chaff, gold without alloy, water without contamination; the word demands that genuine religion have no admixture of self-deception, worldliness, or performance for human approval

Hebrew mishpat and chesed — justice and covenant-love; the two great prophetic categories that define Israel's obligation toward the vulnerable (Micah 6:8; Jer 22:3; Isa 1:17); James's “visiting orphans and widows” is the New Testament application of the Old Testament prophetic demand

Latin religio — scrupulousness, conscientiousness, the binding sense of obligation to the divine; from religare (to bind again); the word implies the obligation is not optional or performative but binding on the conscience — exactly the character of James's definition, which is not a suggestion but a definition of what genuine piety consists in

Usage

"The great Reformation catechisms treated care for the poor and vulnerable as a direct application of the Eighth Commandment (Heidelberg Catechism Q&A 111) and the summary law of love — not as a separate “social gospel” track but as the ordinary outworking of the faith that was justified before God; pure religion and justifying faith are not competitors but the root and the fruit."

"The 1689 Baptist Confession's chapter on Religious Worship (22.1) grounds all right worship in Scripture's prescription, which includes the whole counsel of God — meaning that the believer's obligation to the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner is as much a matter of worship as prayer and the Lord's Supper; James 1:27 is not a social sidebar but a definition of what God-pleasing religion looks like from the outside."

"John Calvin's exposition of Micah 6:8 emphasizes that the prophet is not teaching a minimal religion without ceremony but that ritual obedience without justice and mercy is unacceptable to God — which is precisely James's point: the pure religion is not less than worship but more than worship-without-life; the whole person, directed toward God and neighbor, is what pure religion produces."
